concepts.title: Motion Field from Camera Translation
concepts.one_liner: The 2D motion field for a translating camera relates image velocity to camera velocity and scene depth.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how camera translation generates image motion is fundamental for computer vision tasks like structure from motion. It allows us to relate the physical movement of a camera to the perceived velocity of pixels in the image plane.
concepts.recap_md: - Camera translation creates a motion field where image velocity is inversely proportional to depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: The 2D motion field by using equation is: $$\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}\dot{x} \\\dot{y}\end{bmatrix}= \frac{1}{Z}\begin{bmatrix}-f & 0 & x \\0 & -f & y \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}V_X\\V_Y \\V_Z \end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: Let's now assume that the scene is static and that only the camera is moving. In this case, all the observed motion in the image will be due to the motion of the camera.

concepts.title: Lateral Camera Motion and Parallax
concepts.one_liner: Lateral camera motion occurs when the camera moves parallel to the image plane, creating a parallax effect where closer objects appear to move faster.
concepts.motivation_md: Lateral motion isolates the effect of depth on image velocity. By observing how fast objects move relative to one another during lateral translation, a system can infer their relative distances (parallax).
concepts.recap_md: - Lateral motion occurs when $V_Z = 0$, resulting in image velocity inversely proportional to depth.

key_passage.text: Objects close to the camera will appear moving faster than objects farther away. Objects that are very far will appear as not moving. This parallax effect is the same one used in stereo vision to recover depth.

motivation.text: This parallax effect is the same one used in stereo vision to recover depth.

concepts.title: Focus of Expansion
concepts.one_liner: The focus of expansion is the point in the image where the observed motion is zero during camera translation.
concepts.motivation_md: The focus of expansion identifies the camera's heading. It is a critical cue for navigation and obstacle avoidance, as it indicates the point toward which the camera is moving.
concepts.recap_md: - The focus of expansion is the stationary point $(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})$ in the motion field.

key_passage.text: The observed motion is zero at the focus of expansion, (x_∞, y_∞).

motivation.text: Second, the observed motion only depends on the ratio V_Z/Z, which is the inverse of the time to contact.

concepts.title: Time to Contact
concepts.one_liner: Time to contact is the time required for a moving camera to reach an object at a specific distance.
concepts.content: The observed motion in a forward-moving camera depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact. The time to contact, $Z/V_Z$, is the time it will take the camera to reach an object located at a distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$. Notably, the rate of expansion in the image plane does not depend on the focal length $f$, only on this ratio.
concepts.motivation_md: Time to contact is a vital metric for autonomous systems to avoid collisions, as it provides a temporal measure of proximity that is independent of absolute distance or camera focal length.
concepts.recap_md: - Time to contact is defined as the ratio $Z/V_Z$.

key_passage.text: The time to contact, $V_Z/Z$, is the time it will take the camera to reach the object located a distance $Z$ when moving at velocity $V_Z$.

motivation.text: Second, the observed motion only depends on the ratio $V_Z/Z$, which is the inverse of the time to contact.

concepts.title: Motion Field from Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The motion field for a camera undergoing both translation and rotation relates 2D image velocity to 3D linear and angular velocities.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world camera motion is rarely purely translational. Modeling the combined effects of translation and rotation is necessary to accurately interpret optical flow in complex scenarios like handheld filming or vehicle navigation.
concepts.recap_md: - The motion field is the sum of a translational component (dependent on depth $Z$) and a rotational component (independent of $Z$).

concepts.title: Motion Field under Pure Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: Under pure camera rotation, the 2D motion field is independent of the 3D scene structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between rotational and translational motion is crucial because only translation provides depth cues. Understanding pure rotation helps in calibrating camera parameters and stabilizing images.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure rotation fields are independent of scene depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: The first thing to notice is that the 2D motion field does not depend on the 3D scene structure, Z, and it is only a function of the rotational velocity and the camera parameters. Therefore, under camera rotation we can not learn anything about the scene by observing the motion field. The only thing we can learn from the 2D motion field is about the motion of the camera.

concepts.title: Motion under Varying Focal Length
concepts.one_liner: Changing the focal length of a static camera produces a motion field that scales the image without providing depth information.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights that not all image motion is caused by physical movement. It warns that 'zooming' can mimic the expansion of forward motion but lacks the parallax necessary for depth perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Changing focal length results in a radial scaling of the image plane.

key_passage.text: changing the focal length only results in a scaling of the projected image on the image plane. It does not create any parallax.

concepts.title: Introduction to 3D Motion Projection
concepts.one_liner: Understanding how 3D motion projects into the 2D camera plane is necessary to distinguish between moving cameras and moving objects.
concepts.content: As objects or the camera move, the projection of the dynamic scene into the two-dimensional (2D) camera plane produces a sequence of temporally varying pixel brightness. Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects into the camera allows us to understand the difference between a moving camera and a moving object, and what types of constraints can be used to estimate motion.
concepts.motivation_md: Establishing how physical movement translates to image changes is a prerequisite for developing algorithms that can accurately estimate motion from video data.
concepts.recap_md: - 2D motion in images is a projection of 3D motion in the world.

key_passage.text: Studying how three-dimensional (3D) motion projects into the camera will allow us to understand what the difference is between a moving camera or a moving object and what types of constraints one might be able to use to estimate motion.

motivation.text: Before diving into how to estimate motion from pixels, it is useful to understand the image formation process.

concepts.title: 3D Motion Projection
concepts.one_liner: 3D motion projection defines the relationship between the instantaneous 3D velocity of a point and its corresponding 2D velocity in the image plane.
concepts.content: A 3D point follows a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$ with an instantaneous 3D velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. Its projection into the image plane location is $\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and moves with the 2D instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$. (see figure: A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.) Using perspective projection equations $x=f X/Z$ and $y=f Y/Z$, the relationship between instantaneous velocity in the camera plane and 3D world coordinates is: $$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\ \dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} \end{aligned}$$ This can be written in matrix form as: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & -x \\ 0 & f & -y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{X} \\ \dot{Y} \\ \dot{Z} \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$${#eq-motionprojection}
concepts.motivation_md: This mathematical model is fundamental for computer vision tasks that require recovering 3D information or predicting image changes from known physical motion.
concepts.recap_md: - The 2D velocity of a projected point depends on its 3D velocity and its depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: Using the equations of perspective projection x=f X/Z and y=f Y/Z (assuming that the camera is at the origin of the world-coordinate system), we can derive the equations of how the instantaneous velocity in the camera plane relates to the point motion in 3D world coordinates: $$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= f \frac{\dot{X} Z - \dot{Z} X}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{X} - \dot{Z} x}{Z}\\ \dot{y} &= f \frac{\dot{Y} Z - \dot{Z} Y}{Z^2} = \frac{f \dot{Y} - \dot{Z} y}{Z} \end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: As the point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The projection of this point into the image plane location is $\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$.

concepts.title: Properties of Optical Flow
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow properties describe how 3D motion, such as lateral or longitudinal movement, projects into specific velocity patterns on the image plane.
concepts.content: The motion projection equations reveal interesting properties of optical flow. Points moving parallel to the camera plane ($\dot{Z} = 0$) project to a motion parallel to the 3D motion with a magnitude inversely proportional to the distance $Z$: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{f}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{X} \\ \dot{Y} \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$${#eq-parallelmotion} For points moving parallel to the $Z$ axis ($\dot{X} = \dot{Y} = 0$), the projection is: $$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{\dot{Z}}{Z} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$${#eq-forward_objects} Points at the same distance $Z$ moving toward or away from the camera with the same velocity will project into points moving at different velocities on the image plane depending on their $(x, y)$ location. (see figure: (left) Geometry of the projection of 3D motion into the camera for points moving parallel to the camera plane, and (right) parallel to the optical axis of the camera.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these properties allows us to infer depth information and movement direction from the patterns of motion observed in a 2D image sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - For lateral motion, image velocity is inversely proportional to depth $Z$.

key_passage.text: This expression reveals a number of interesting properties of the optical flow and how it relates to motion in the world. For instance, points that move parallel to the camera plane ($\dot{Z} = 0$) will project to a motion parallel to the motion in 3D but with a magnitude that will be inversely proportional to the distance $Z$

concepts.title: Vanishing Point in Motion
concepts.one_liner: A vanishing point in motion is the image location where a point moving in a straight 3D line with constant velocity converges as time approaches infinity.
concepts.content: For a point moving in a straight line in 3D with constant velocity $\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (V_X, V_Y, V_Z)^\mathsf{T}$, its location at time $t$ is $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X+V_Xt, Y+V_Yt, Z+V_Zt)^\mathsf{T}$. If $\dot{Z} \neq 0$, then as time goes to infinity, the projected point converges to a vanishing point: $$\begin{aligned} \lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) &= f \frac{V_X}{V_Z} = x_{\infty}\\ \lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) &= f \frac{V_Y}{V_Z} = y_{\infty} \end{aligned}$${#eq-motionvanishingpoint} (see figure: Projection onto the camera plane of the sequence produced by a bird flying away. The bird will vanish at the **vanishing point**) The location of the vanishing point $\mathbf{p}_{\infty}=(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})^\mathsf{T}$ is independent of the initial point location and depends only on the 3D velocity vector $\mathbf{V}$. Multiple points moving with the same velocity will converge to the same vanishing point.
concepts.motivation_md: Vanishing points provide a stable reference for determining an observer's heading or identifying groups of objects moving in the same direction in a 3D scene.
concepts.recap_md: - The vanishing point is the limit of a projected trajectory as time goes to infinity.

key_passage.text: The vanishing point is the location $\mathbf{p}_{\infty}=(x_{\infty}, y_{\infty})^\mathsf{T}$ where the moving point slowly converges to. The location of the vanishing point is independent of the point location at time $t=0$, and it only depends on the 3D velocity vector, $\mathbf{V}$.

motivation.text: In the camera the bird gets smaller as it flies away until it disappears at the vanishing point. Therefore, if the scene contains multiple points at different locations moving with the same velocity, they will converge to the same vanishing point.

prereq.rationale: Specific properties of optical flow are derived from the general motion projection equations.
The motion field for a translating camera is a specific application of the general 3D motion projection equations.
The focus of expansion is defined based on the motion field equations for a translating camera.
Time to contact is derived from the rate of expansion observed in the motion field during forward translation.
The motion field for varying focal length is derived by taking the temporal derivative of the projection equation with respect to f.

overlay.rationale: Lateral motion is a specific case of camera translation where the forward velocity is zero.
The general motion field combines both translation and rotation components.
Pure rotation is the case where the translation vector in the general motion field is zero.
Unlike camera translation, changing focal length produces a motion field that is independent of scene depth.
